name: Skytable
workload: GET/SET requests via redis-benchmark/memtier/sky-bench, 30 threads with 1 client per thread, run against Redis, KeyDB, Dragonfly and Skytable on two AWS m5.4xlarge instances (one server, one client)
claimed_speedup: GET/SET ops/sec: Skytable 619,992/676,091 vs Redis 112,100/99,892 (~5.5-6.8x); also ahead of KeyDB (288,931/282,997) and Dragonfly (408,322/392,446)
hardware: 2x AWS m5.4xlarge (one running the k/v store, one running the benchmark client)
tradeoffs: Skytable answers queries in BlueQL (a small SQL-like language) rather than plain GET/SET, so it does strictly more parsing/validation work per request than Redis/KeyDB yet still came out ahead in this benchmark; this 0.8.x line is single-node only (clustering was still WIP at the time); Skytable is also the only one of the four that runs natively on Windows.
caveats: Benchmarker states no affiliation with any of the four projects and ran the tests themselves (redis-benchmark, memtier_benchmark, sky-bench) on 2x m5.4xlarge, but reports Skytable's numbers were 'a little inconsistent at times' and that they could NOT reproduce Dragonfly's own claimed 25x-over-Redis speedup. Compiler/build flags for the four server binaries are not stated. Skytable's own first-party benchmark repo (github.com/ohsayan/sky-benches, same author as Skytable) shows a similar Redis/KeyDB/Skytable comparison on a 6C/12T Tiger Lake box with hardware specified but is first-party, not used as the primary citation here.
found_via: HN Algolia search 'Redis KeyDB Dragonfly Skytable' -> HN item 31796311 'Redis vs. KeyDB vs. Dragonfly vs. Skytable' (independent shootout, 130 points)

name: EloqKV
workload: memtier_benchmark write-only (ratio 1:0), read-only (ratio 0:1), and mixed (ratio 1:10 put:get) workloads against a single-node in-memory-only (persistence/WAL disabled) instance, 128-byte values, 5,000,000-key keyspace, concurrency swept from 128 to 1024 (32 threads x 4/8/16/32 clients), 300s test runs
claimed_speedup: 'EloqKV and DragonflyDB both outperform Redis due to their support for multiple worker threads' on throughput and p99.9 latency across write-only, read-only and mixed workloads; EloqKV throughput/latency described as 'almost the same' as DragonflyDB and both 'significantly outperform Redis' -- exact ops/sec are shown only as chart images on the source page, not printed as text
hardware: AWS EC2, region us-east-1, Ubuntu 22.04: server = c7g.8xlarge (Graviton, ARM64) running Redis 7.2.5 / DragonflyDB 1.21.2 / EloqKV 0.7.4 one at a time; client = c6gn.8xlarge running memtier_benchmark
tradeoffs: EloqKV splits compute/logging/storage into separate services (TxService + LogService + Storage Service) and enables io_uring by default, requiring --privileged and custom ulimits in Docker; adds full ACID distributed transactions (BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK, cross-node, no CROSSSLOT) that Redis lacks, at the cost of architectural complexity; for this specific cache-mode benchmark EloqKV had its own persistent storage and WAL turned off to make the comparison to Redis/DragonflyDB fair, so it does not exercise EloqKV's durability path.
caveats: This is a first-party benchmark authored and run by EloqData (the company behind EloqKV), not an independent third party -- per methodology it is capped at tier C despite detailed hardware/version/command documentation. Live URL eloqdata.com/blog/2024/08/17/benchmark-single-node returns HTTP 404 as of 2026-09-26 (blog appears to have been restructured); content was recovered via a Wayback Machine snapshot dated 2026-06-16. No compiler or build flags are given for any of the three server binaries. License field is NOASSERTION on the GitHub API; the repo's LICENSE file states a dual GPLv2-or-AGPLv3 choice.
found_via: HN Algolia search 'kvrocks' surfaced 'Show HN: EloqKV - Scalable distributed ACID key-value database with Redis API' -> github.com/eloqdata/eloqkv README 'Benchmark' section -> linked blog post (recovered via web.archive.org)

name: Valkey
workload: valkey-benchmark: 50M SET operations followed by 50M GET operations, 1KB item values, 3,000,000-key keyspace, ~500 connections (tuned per system), single node, --threads 6
claimed_speedup: Valkey 8.1.1 999.8K RPS on SET @0.8ms p99 vs Redis 8.0 729.4K RPS on SET @0.99ms p99 (37% higher SET throughput); ~16% higher GET throughput and '60%+ faster' p99 read latencies vs Redis (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: valkey-benchmark run with --threads 6; compiler/build flags for the Valkey and Redis server binaries themselves are not stated
hardware: AWS Graviton4-based c8g.2xlarge (8 vCPU) server in an EC2 cluster placement group; c8g.8xlarge (32 vCPU) load generator
tradeoffs: Valkey originated as a community fork of Redis (created when Redis relicensed away from BSD) and has since added its own multi-threaded I/O path in the 8.x line, which is the source of this speedup; API/RESP-protocol compatible so migration cost from Redis is low, but as with any fork it can diverge over time from upstream Redis modules and Redis Enterprise-only features.
caveats: Momento (the blog's publisher) is a caching-as-a-service vendor that also sells Valkey-based products (valkey-router, valkey-operator), so it is not a fully neutral third party even though it is independent of the Valkey project itself; the article includes a 'Try it Yourself' reproduction section but does not link a public benchmark-code repository, so it falls short of tier A. A secondary aggregator blog (andrewbaker.ninja, 2026-01-04) cites the same 37%/999.8K-RPS figures, corroborating they were not altered in transmission.
